plots.title: Drag of the rider silhouette (wake-deficit estimate)
plots.explain: APPROXIMATION: drag of the rider silhouette estimated from the wake momentum deficit at one plane (x = 801 cells) with the velocity clipped to [0, U] — C_d ≈ (2/D)∫(u/U)(1−u/U)dy — normalised by the reference length D. It excludes the bypass flow and pressure terms, so it indicates trends (bigger wake → more drag) rather than a validated force coefficient. A boundary-force (momentum-exchange) evaluation is the quantitative route and is not implemented.

plots.title: Lift signal
plots.explain: Transverse velocity at a point in the wake (wake probe, sampled every lattice step); its oscillation is the alternating side force of vortex shedding. Units: lattice velocity. Source: the solver's wake probe written every step, after the first 20 % of the run (start-up transient removed).

lbm_cyclist.name: Rider Silhouette
lbm_cyclist.question: How large is the wake behind a single rider?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How large is the wake behind a single rider?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A rider in a tucked position, as a 2-D silhouette on a road. A stagnation region forms in front and a wide wake of shed vortices trails behind.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Open the Drafting scene to put a second rider in this wake.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The wake width and the slipstream profile downstream.
fixed: Obstacle size: Re is held: ν is recomputed from the new D
Reynolds number: U and D stay; ν = U·D/Re changes
Inflow speed: Re stays; ν changes with U

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
Put any object in a steady stream and the flow has to go around it. Past a critical Reynolds number the boundary layers on the object's sides separate, form a pair of shear layers, and those layers become unstable: one rolls up into a vortex, grows until it pulls the opposite layer across the wake, sheds downstream, and the process repeats on the other side. The result is a staggered, periodic train of counter-rotating vortices — the von Kármán vortex street.

Each shed vortex throws momentum sideways and pushes back on the body with a force that alternates at the shedding frequency. That is why chimneys, bridge decks, heat-exchanger tubes, antennas and offshore risers can suffer destructive 'vortex-induced vibration', why a wire sings in the wind, and why those swirling cloud streets trail downwind of islands. Swap the cylinder for a square, a sharp diamond, an angled airfoil (which also generates lift), or your own name, and you change where the flow separates — and so the whole wake.

What ties it together is the Reynolds number, Re = U·D/ν, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. Raise it and the wake goes steady → periodic shedding → turbulent; the shedding frequency collapses onto a near-constant Strouhal number St = f·D/U ≈ 0.2. Because lattice-Boltzmann represents the obstacle as a set of solid cells on a regular lattice, any shape drops in without a body-fitted mesh — one reason LBM is used for flow through geometrically complex media.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• fq — the population of fluid 'walkers' moving along lattice direction q
• cq — the discrete velocity of direction q (one of 9 in D2Q9)
• fq^eq — the local equilibrium (a discretised Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution)
• τ — the relaxation time; how fast populations relax toward equilibrium. It sets the viscosity through ν = (τ − ½)/3
• left side — streaming: each population hops to the neighbouring cell
• right side — collision: populations relax toward equilibrium
• the obstacle is just the cells flagged solid — a shape, or the pixels of your text

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Uniform flow at the inflow speed everywhere (equilibrium populations); a brief transverse inflow perturbation seeds the wake instability.
layers.bc: Velocity inlet on the left, zero-gradient outflow on the right with a relaxation sponge over the last 12 % (it reduces but does not eliminate reflections), periodic top and bottom, and no-slip half-way bounce-back on the obstacle. Vehicle scenes add a no-slip road.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: Solved with a D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann method: nine discrete velocities per cell, a single-relaxation-time (BGK) collision toward the local equilibrium, and a streaming step that shifts populations to neighbours. The obstacle — any shape or text — is simply a set of cells flagged solid and handled by half-way bounce-back (a no-slip wall); obstacles are represented on the regular lattice, so a body-fitted mesh is unnecessary. Velocity inlet, zero-gradient outflow, periodic top/bottom; the relaxation time τ sets the viscosity via ν = (τ − ½)/3, hence the Reynolds number.
layers.checks: Qualitative demonstration (2-D, low Reynolds number). No real-world power figures are computed.

layers.title: References
items: Krüger, T. et al. (2017). The Lattice Boltzmann Method: Principles and Practice. Springer.

obstacle.label: Obstacle
obstacle.help: What to drop into the stream — a shape, a vehicle, or your own text.

text.label: Your text
text.help: The word to drop into the stream. Short words read best.

size.label: Obstacle size
size.help: Obstacle size (cylinder diameter, square side, airfoil chord/2.6) as a fraction of the channel height. Bigger → larger, slower-shedding wake.
size.fixed: Re is held: ν is recomputed from the new D

angle.label: Airfoil angle of attack
angle.help: Angle of attack in degrees; positive = leading edge up (lift upward). Negative angles mirror the flow and give downward lift.

reynolds.label: Reynolds number
reynolds.help: Reynolds number Re = U·D/ν (inertia ÷ viscosity) with D the reference length below. Low → smooth steady flow; high → vortex shedding and turbulence.
reynolds.fixed: U and D stay; ν = U·D/Re changes

speed.label: Inflow speed
speed.help: Inlet flow speed in lattice units. The Reynolds number is held fixed: the viscosity is recomputed as ν = U·D/Re, so a higher speed means a higher lattice Mach number (keep ≲ 0.15) and a shorter physical time per step, not a stronger wake.
speed.fixed: Re stays; ν changes with U

xpos.label: Obstacle position
xpos.help: Streamwise position of the obstacle centre as a fraction of the tunnel length.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).

compare.text: Isolated rider versus two riders at the same speed; the combined wake-deficit drag is an approximation.
